title: Fifteen thousand year old clay birds rewrite the story of symbolic art in Southwest Asia
dek: A re-examination of museum collections reveals 154 clay objects from three Natufian sites, pushing the region's figurative tradition back into the Epipalaeolithic.
body: You hold a lump of clay the size of a thumbnail. It has been heated, coloured with red ochre, and shaped into a waterfowl with its neck curved downward in a courtship display. A fingerprint presses into the clay where a thumb smoothed the slip. This is not a Neolithic farmer's work. It was made by a hunter-gatherer 15,000 years ago on the slopes of Mount Carmel.

Archaeologists recovered the artefacts from el-Wad Terrace, Hayonim Terrace in Galilee, and Eynan-Mallaha in the Upper Jordan Valley. The pieces sat in collections for decades, catalogued as debris from pigment production. A team re-examined tens of thousands of heated clay fragments and identified 15 complete figurines alongside 139 cylindrical fragments interpreted as body parts and appendages.

Eleven of the figurines are birds. Several show the cylindrical necks and downward-facing heads of waterfowl such as ducks, geese, or swans. Others may depict birds of prey. Two fragments represent hoofed animals, one possibly a mountain gazelle with small impressions suggesting twigs were inserted for horns. If confirmed, this would be among the earliest composite figurines in Southwest Asia, combining clay with perishable materials.

Two human forms appear in the assemblage. One shows the upper body with modelled arms. The other is a stylised face that may have held decorations of grass, fibre, hair, or feathers. Microscopic examination reveals fingerprints, palm impressions, and fingertip depressions from shaping, smoothing, grooving, and incision. The marks show that children as well as adults made these objects.

Ten of the eleven bird figurines carry traces of red colouring. One Early Natufian example was coated with an iron-rich clay slip, an engobe technique. An uncoloured diagonal line appears to have been created using a plant fibre as a stencil during application. The study reports this as the earliest known evidence for engobe use in the region.

All objects were heated, though researchers do not know if they were fired intentionally, warmed passively near hearths, or burned accidentally after deposition. Further analysis will investigate their heating histories and exposure temperatures. Prior to this study, only two clay figurines had been identified in the Natufian record. Figurative clay use was generally associated with later Neolithic societies.

The recurrence of similar forms across three sites separated by distance indicates an established figurative tradition rather than isolated experiments. Researchers say the findings push part of Southwest Asia's so-called revolution of symbols back into Epipalaeolithic times. Developments in symbolic expression and clay technology were already underway before agriculture emerged.
doesnt_show: The study does not show whether the figurines served ritual, social, or playful functions. It does not establish that the clay was fired intentionally as pottery. The composite interpretation for the gazelle fragment relies on small impressions that could have other causes.
settle: Controlled firing experiments and residue analysis on the gazelle fragment would clarify manufacturing intent and the composite hypothesis.
